site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Refuge on the Shore of Compassion
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana — Yuddha Kanda (Gita Press translation)
body: Vibhishana, brother of Ravana, pleaded in Lanka for Sita's return and an end to the coming war. When Ravana scorned his counsel and cast him out, Vibhishana flew across the sea with four loyal companions and landed in Rama's camp, seeking shelter from the prince of Ayodhya.

Among the vanara generals, suspicion rose, for the newcomer was kin to the enemy king. Rama listened to the worried voices, then spoke with quiet certainty: anyone who comes seeking refuge with a sincere heart must be protected, even from an opposing host.

Welcomed into the army, Vibhishana was anointed by the sea-god's waters as the rightful future king of Lanka. The war camp found in him a wise counselor, and Rama's choice turned mercy itself into a guiding principle, stronger than any fear.

stories.title: Kishkindha Welcomes Its King Again
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana — Kishkindha Kanda (Gita Press translation)
body: Hanuman led Rama through the forest paths to the exiled prince Sugriva, and a warm pact was forged between them: Rama would help Sugriva reclaim Kishkindha, and Sugriva's vanara forces would search every corner of the earth for Sita. Trust settled between them like a steady lamp.

When Sugriva faced his brother Vali in a renewed duel, Rama stood beside his ally, and Vali fell. With his final breath, Vali placed his son Angada into the care of Rama and Sugriva, entrusting the boy to their joined protection.

Sugriva was crowned king of Kishkindha, with young Angada named heir, and the reunited vanara hosts prepared to march across the world seeking Sita. The forest kingdom stood peaceful again, and the friendship between Rama and Sugriva shone bright as the search began.

stories.title: The Note Honored in Dwarka
body: Narsinh Mehta, the poet-saint whose heart belonged to Krishna, welcomed a band of weary pilgrims to his home and worried how to see them onward. With quiet faith he sat down and wrote a hundi, a promissory note payable in the holy city of Dwarka, trusting the Lord to honor it in some unseen way.

When the travelers reached Dwarka, a merchant named Shamal Shah read the note and, without hesitation, paid the full sum as though he had been expecting them. The pilgrims were cared for, fed, and sent on their journey with enough for their road, their debt settled by a stranger's generous hand.

Returning home, they bowed before Narsinh and poured out their thanks for the kind merchant in Dwarka. The saint only smiled, for he understood at once that Krishna himself had come as Shamal Shah to keep the promise. In that recognition, devotion and hospitality became one, and the small household rejoiced in a love that never fails.

stories.title: Bhima Finds His Elder Brother
stories.source: Mahabharata — Vana Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
body: During the Pandavas' forest exile, Draupadi noticed a fragrant celestial lotus and asked Bhima to bring her more. He set off toward the mountain sacred to Kubera, striding loudly through the wild path. Ahead, an old monkey lay resting, his long tail stretched across the road.

Bhima asked the monkey to move, but the creature only smiled and invited him to lift the tail himself. Confident in his famous strength, Bhima seized it and pulled with all his might. The tail would not budge. Humbled, he realized he stood before Hanuman, elder son of the wind-god and brother he had never known.

Hanuman revealed his radiant, sky-filling form and blessed his younger brother with renewed strength. He promised to aid the Pandavas' cause by resting upon Arjuna's banner in the war to come. Bhima returned to his family wiser at heart, carrying quiet hope for the days ahead.

stories.title: Hanuman Finds Sita
body: After leaping across the ocean, Hanuman slipped into Lanka and searched until he found Sita in the Ashoka grove, where she sat faithful and sorrowful. From a safe branch, he softly spoke Rama's name, letting the sound reach her like the first breeze after a long wait.

Sita lifted her gaze, hope trembling in her eyes, as Hanuman descended and offered Rama's ring as proof that her beloved had truly sent him. Overjoyed, she pressed a jewel into his hand and whispered a message of love and longing to carry back across the sea.

Hanuman bowed, tucked the jewel close, and bounded away toward the waiting vanara army, his heart full of news. With every stride over the water, he carried Sita's courage and Rama's promise, and soon the whole forest would learn that hope had finally been found.
